subtopic: Moment of Inertia and Radius of Gyration
stem: The MI of ring of radius \(R\) and mass \(M\) about its central axis is _____
solution:
**(C)** \(MR^{2}\)

The central axis of a ring is the axis through its centre, perpendicular to its plane. Every mass element of the ring lies at the same distance \(R\) from this axis.

\(I = \sum m_i r_i^{2} = R^{2}\sum m_i = MR^{2}\)

\(\therefore\) the moment of inertia is \(MR^{2}\).

The distractors are the neighbouring standard results: \(\dfrac{MR^{2}}{2}\) is a disc about the same axis, and \(\dfrac{3}{2}MR^{2}\) is a ring about a tangent lying in its own plane.

chapter: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Law of Equipartition of Energy and Degrees of Freedom
stem: For a monoatomic gas enclosed in a container at a constant temperature has degrees of freedom
solution:
**(B)** 3

A monoatomic gas molecule is a single atom and is treated as a point mass. It can move along the three coordinate directions, so it has three translational degrees of freedom. Having no extension, it carries no rotational kinetic energy about any axis, and being a single atom it has no vibrational mode.

\(\therefore\) the number of degrees of freedom is \(f = 3\).

A diatomic molecule at ordinary temperature has 5 (three translational plus two rotational), which is the distractor offered.

stem: The equation of the first law of thermodynamics for isochoric process is
solution:
**(A)** \(Q = \Delta U\)

The first law of thermodynamics is \(Q = \Delta U + W\), where \(W\) is the work done by the system.

In an isochoric process the volume is constant, so \(\Delta V = 0\) and

\(W = \displaystyle\int p\,dV = 0\)

Substituting \(W = 0\),

\(\therefore Q = \Delta U\); all the heat supplied goes into raising the internal energy.

chapter: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
stem: Cyclotron can not accelerate _____
solution:
**(C)** neutrons

A cyclotron works by two effects acting together: a magnetic field bends the particle into a circular path through the force \(qvB\), and an alternating electric field across the dees accelerates it each half revolution. Both forces are proportional to the charge \(q\).

A neutron carries no charge, so \(q = 0\) and it experiences neither force.

\(\therefore\) a cyclotron cannot accelerate neutrons. Protons, deuterons and \(\alpha\)-particles are all charged and can be accelerated.

stem: In a purely inductive and capacitive circuit, power factor is, _____
solution:
**(B)** zero

Power factor is \(\cos\phi\), where \(\phi\) is the phase angle between the applied voltage and the current.

In a purely inductive circuit the current lags the voltage by \(90^{\circ}\); in a purely capacitive circuit it leads by \(90^{\circ}\). In either case \(\phi = 90^{\circ}\).

\(\cos 90^{\circ} = 0\)

\(\therefore\) the power factor is zero. Such a circuit consumes no average power over a cycle and is called a wattless circuit.

stem: The Boolean equation for NOR gate is
solution:
**(D)** \(Y = \overline{A + B}\)

A NOR gate is an OR gate followed by a NOT gate, so its output is the complement of the OR output.

OR gives \(A + B\); negating it gives \(Y = \overline{A + B}\).

\(\therefore\) the Boolean equation of the NOR gate is \(Y = \overline{A + B}\).

Of the others, \(Y = A \cdot B\) is AND, \(Y = A + B\) is OR, and \(Y = \overline{A}\) is NOT.

stem: When \(n\) number of capacitors having each of capacity \(C\) are connected in series, their equivalent capacity is
solution:
**(C)** \(\dfrac{C}{n}\)

For capacitors in series the reciprocals of the capacities add. With \(n\) capacitors each of capacity \(C\),

\(\dfrac{1}{C_s} = \dfrac{1}{C} + \dfrac{1}{C} + \cdots\) (\(n\) terms) \(= \dfrac{n}{C}\)

\(\therefore C_s = \dfrac{C}{n}\)

The series combination is therefore smaller than any single capacitor. Note that \(\dfrac{1}{nC}\) is the reciprocal of a capacity and so is not itself a capacity.

stem: A polarising angle for an optical material is 35°. Then refractive index of the material is
solution:
**(B)** 0.7002

By Brewster's law the refractive index and the polarising angle are related by

\(\mu = \tan\theta_p\)

Here \(\theta_p = 35^{\circ}\), so

\(\mu = \tan 35^{\circ} = 0.7002\)

\(\therefore\) the refractive index of the material is \(0.7002\).

subtopic: Viscosity, Critical Velocity and Reynolds Number
stem: For a streamline flow, the relative velocity between the two liquid layers is 10 cm/s. The distance between them is 5 cm. The velocity gradient is
solution:
**(D)** \(2\ \text{S}^{-1}\)

The velocity gradient is the rate of change of layer velocity with distance across the flow:

\(\text{velocity gradient} = \dfrac{dv}{dx} = \dfrac{\text{relative velocity}}{\text{separation}}\)

\(= \dfrac{10\ \text{cm/s}}{5\ \text{cm}} = 2\) per second

The centimetres cancel, so no unit conversion is needed.

\(\therefore\) the velocity gradient is \(2\ \text{S}^{-1}\) as printed.

stem: The wavelength of a stationary wave on a string is 0.75 m with frequency of 64 Hz. Then, the velocity of wave is
solution:
**(A)** 48 m/s

For any wave the velocity, frequency and wavelength are related by

\(v = n\lambda\)

Here \(n = 64\ \text{Hz}\) and \(\lambda = 0.75\ \text{m}\), so

\(v = 64 \times 0.75 = 48\ \text{m/s}\)

\(\therefore\) the velocity of the wave is \(48\ \text{m/s}\).

stem: Absorption of ink by a blotting paper is an example of which phenomenon of fluids?
solution:
Absorption of ink by blotting paper is an example of **capillarity** (capillary action).

The blotting paper is a mesh of fine pores which behave as narrow capillary tubes. Ink wets the fibres, so its angle of contact is acute, and the resulting surface tension force draws the liquid up into the pores.

stem: State Kirchhoff's first law for electrical network.
solution:
**Kirchhoff's first law (the junction law):** the algebraic sum of the currents meeting at any junction in an electrical network is zero.

\(\sum I = 0\)

Equivalently, the total current flowing into a junction equals the total current flowing out of it. The law is a statement of conservation of electric charge, since charge cannot accumulate at a junction.

chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: Define 'photoelectric work function.'
solution:
The **photoelectric work function** of a metal is the minimum energy required to just free an electron from the metal surface, that is, to remove it from the surface without giving it any kinetic energy.

It is written \(\phi_0 = h\nu_0\), where \(\nu_0\) is the threshold frequency of the metal. It is usually expressed in electron volts.

stem: Which series of spectral lines belongs to the ultraviolet region of the hydrogen spectrum?
solution:
The **Lyman series** belongs to the ultraviolet region of the hydrogen spectrum.

Its lines arise from transitions in which the electron falls to the ground state, \(n = 1\), from any higher orbit. These are the largest energy jumps in the hydrogen atom, so they give the shortest wavelengths, which lie in the ultraviolet.

stem: Which semiconductor device converts solar energy into electrical energy?
solution:
A **solar cell** (photovoltaic cell) converts solar energy into electrical energy.

It is a p-n junction diode with a large surface area exposed to light. Photons absorbed near the junction create electron-hole pairs, and the junction field separates them, producing a photovoltage across the cell even with no external bias.

subtopic: Nature of Light and Huygens' Principle
stem: Define the term wavefront.
solution:
A **wavefront** is the locus of all points of a medium that are in the same state of vibration, that is, all points which are oscillating in phase.

Every point of a wavefront has the same phase at a given instant, and the direction of propagation of the wave is everywhere normal to the wavefront. A point source gives spherical wavefronts, which become effectively plane at a great distance.

stem:
A motorcyclist performs horizontal circular motion inside a well of inner radius 3 m. Calculate the minimum speed to perform the stunt if coefficient of static friction is 0.3.
[ \(g = 10\ \text{m/s}^{2}\) ].
solution:
For a motorcyclist on the inside wall of a well of death, the normal reaction is horizontal and supplies the centripetal force, while the force of static friction acts vertically upward and balances the weight.

\(N = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}\) and \(\mu_s N = mg\)

Dividing, \(\mu_s \dfrac{v^{2}}{r} = g\), so

\(v_{\min} = \sqrt{\dfrac{rg}{\mu_s}}\)

Substituting \(r = 3\ \text{m}\), \(g = 10\ \text{m/s}^{2}\) and \(\mu_s = 0.3\),

\(v_{\min} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3 \times 10}{0.3}} = \sqrt{100} = 10\ \text{m/s}\)

\(\therefore\) the minimum speed needed to perform the stunt is \(10\ \text{m/s}\).

subtopic: Acceleration, Velocity and Displacement in S.H.M.
stem: Calculate the maximum velocity of a particle having amplitude of oscillation 4 cm and period 4 seconds.
solution:
For a particle in linear S.H.M. the speed is greatest at the mean position, where

\(v_{\max} = A\omega = A \times \dfrac{2\pi}{T}\)

Here \(A = 4\ \text{cm} = 0.04\ \text{m}\) and \(T = 4\ \text{s}\), so

\(\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{4} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\ \text{rad/s}\)

\(v_{\max} = 0.04 \times \dfrac{\pi}{2} = 0.02\pi = 0.0628\ \text{m/s}\)

\(\therefore\) the maximum velocity is \(0.0628\ \text{m/s}\), that is \(6.28\ \text{cm/s}\).

stem: Obtain an expression for the maximum speed of a vehicle along horizontal circular curved road.
solution:
Consider a vehicle of mass \(m\) taking a turn of radius \(r\) on a level (unbanked) road. The road is horizontal, so the normal reaction balances the weight:

\(N = mg\)

The only horizontal force available to supply the centripetal force is the force of static friction between the tyres and the road, directed toward the centre:

\(f_s = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}\)

Static friction cannot exceed its limiting value \(\mu_s N = \mu_s mg\). The speed is therefore greatest when friction is at that limit:

\(\dfrac{mv_{\max}^{2}}{r} = \mu_s mg\)

The mass cancels, giving

\(\therefore v_{\max} = \sqrt{\mu_s r g}\)

The maximum safe speed is independent of the mass of the vehicle and depends only on the coefficient of static friction, the radius of the turn and \(g\).

subtopic: Thermodynamic State Variables and the p-V Diagram
stem:
For a thermodynamic system :
Define :
(a) Mechanical equilibrium
(b) Chemical equilibrium
solution:
**(a) Mechanical equilibrium:** a thermodynamic system is in mechanical equilibrium when there is no unbalanced force within the system, and none between the system and its surroundings. The pressure is then the same throughout the system and equal to that of the surroundings, so no part of the system accelerates and no volume change occurs.

**(b) Chemical equilibrium:** a system is in chemical equilibrium when its chemical composition does not change with time. There is no net chemical reaction and no net transfer of matter from one part of the system to another or across its boundary.

stem: What are polar molecules and non polar molecules?
solution:
**Polar molecules:** molecules in which the centre of positive charge and the centre of negative charge do not coincide, even when no external electric field is applied. Such a molecule has a permanent electric dipole moment. This happens when the constituent atoms differ in electronegativity and the shape of the molecule is unsymmetrical. Water, \(HCl\) and \(NH_3\) are polar.

**Non polar molecules:** molecules in which the centres of positive and negative charge coincide, so the molecule has no permanent dipole moment. These are usually symmetrical molecules. \(H_2\), \(O_2\), \(CO_2\) and \(CH_4\) are non polar. In an external field their charge centres separate slightly and an induced dipole moment appears.

stem: Explain how will you convert moving coil galvanometer into voltmeter?
solution:
A moving coil galvanometer is converted into a voltmeter by connecting a **high resistance in series** with it.

Let the galvanometer have resistance \(G\) and let \(I_g\) be the current for full scale deflection. To read voltages up to \(V\), a resistance \(X\) is placed in series so that the whole of \(V\) is dropped across the combination when the current through it is \(I_g\):

\(V = I_g(G + X)\)

\(\therefore X = \dfrac{V}{I_g} - G\)

Because \(X\) is large, the resistance of the voltmeter is high, so when it is connected across a circuit element it draws very little current and disturbs the circuit as little as possible. An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance.

stem: Distinguish between free and forced vibrations.
solution:
| Free vibrations | Forced vibrations |
|---|---|
| The body vibrates on its own after a single initial disturbance, with no periodic external force acting afterwards. | The body vibrates under the action of a periodic external force applied continuously. |
| The frequency is the natural frequency of the body, fixed by its own inertia and elasticity. | The frequency is that of the applied periodic force, not the natural frequency of the body. |
| In the absence of damping the amplitude stays constant; in practice damping makes it die away. | The amplitude stays constant as long as the external force acts, the energy lost to damping being replaced by that force. |
| Example: a tuning fork sounding after being struck once. | Example: the body of a sonometer set vibrating by a tuning fork pressed on it. |

When the frequency of the applied force equals the natural frequency of the body, the forced vibrations have maximum amplitude and the phenomenon is called resonance.

stem: State any two postulates of Bohr's theory of hydrogen atom.
solution:
Two of the postulates of Bohr's theory of the hydrogen atom are:

**1. The stationary orbits.** An electron revolves round the nucleus only in certain allowed circular orbits, in which its angular momentum is an integral multiple of \(\dfrac{h}{2\pi}\):

\(mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}\), where \(n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\)

While in such an orbit the electron does not radiate energy, even though it is accelerated. These are called stationary orbits or energy states.

**2. The frequency condition.** The atom radiates or absorbs energy only when the electron jumps from one stationary orbit to another. If it falls from an orbit of energy \(E_2\) to one of energy \(E_1\), a single photon is emitted whose frequency is given by

\(h\nu = E_2 - E_1\)

stem: Explain the cyclic process with the help of a neat \(p-V\) diagram.
solution:
A **cyclic process** is one in which the system, after passing through a series of changes, returns to its initial state. Its initial and final pressure, volume and temperature are therefore the same.

On a \(p\)-\(V\) diagram such a process is represented by a **closed curve**. Suppose the system goes from state A to state B along the upper path and returns from B to A along the lower path, so that the curve is traced clockwise.

Because internal energy is a state function and the system returns to its initial state,

\(\Delta U = 0\)

The first law \(Q = \Delta U + W\) then gives

\(\therefore Q = W\)

All the net heat absorbed in the cycle is converted into net work done by the system. That net work equals the **area enclosed by the closed curve** on the \(p\)-\(V\) diagram: the expansion along the upper path does positive work equal to the area under it, the compression along the lower path does negative work equal to the area under that, and the difference is the enclosed area. A clockwise cycle does positive net work, as in a heat engine; an anticlockwise cycle does negative net work, as in a refrigerator.

stem: A star is emitting light at the wavelength of 4000Å. Determine the limit of angular resolution of a telescope having an objective of diameter of 400 cm.
solution:
The limit of angular resolution of a telescope is set by diffraction at the circular aperture of its objective, and is given by Rayleigh's criterion

\(\theta = \dfrac{1.22\lambda}{D}\)

Here \(\lambda = 4000\ \text{Å} = 4000 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{m} = 4 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}\) and \(D = 400\ \text{cm} = 4\ \text{m}\).

\(\theta = \dfrac{1.22 \times 4 \times 10^{-7}}{4}\)

\(\theta = 1.22 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{rad}\)

\(\therefore\) the limit of angular resolution of the telescope is \(1.22 \times 10^{-7}\) radian. Two stars closer together than this angle cannot be seen as separate.

chapter: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Spectral Distribution and Wien's Displacement Law
stem:
Calculate the value of \(\lambda_{\max}\) for solar radiation assuming the temperature on the surface of the sun is 5800 K.
[ Wien's constant \(= 2.897 \times 10^{-3}\) m.k. ]
solution:
By Wien's displacement law the wavelength at which a black body radiates most strongly is inversely proportional to its absolute temperature:

\(\lambda_{\max} T = b\)

where \(b\) is Wien's constant. Here \(b = 2.897 \times 10^{-3}\) m.k. and \(T = 5800\ \text{K}\).

\(\lambda_{\max} = \dfrac{b}{T} = \dfrac{2.897 \times 10^{-3}}{5800}\)

\(\lambda_{\max} = 4.995 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}\)

\(\therefore \lambda_{\max} = 4.995 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}\), that is about \(4995\ \text{Å}\), which lies in the visible region near the blue-green.

stem:
Calculate the radius of water drop, so that the excess pressure inside it is \(24\ \text{N/m}^{2}\).
[ Surface tension of water \(= 7.2 \times 10^{-2}\) N/m ]
solution:
For a liquid drop there is a single free surface, so the excess pressure inside it is

\(p = \dfrac{2T}{r}\)

Rearranging for the radius,

\(r = \dfrac{2T}{p}\)

Here \(T = 7.2 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{N/m}\) and \(p = 24\ \text{N/m}^{2}\).

\(r = \dfrac{2 \times 7.2 \times 10^{-2}}{24} = \dfrac{14.4 \times 10^{-2}}{24}\)

\(r = 6 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}\)

\(\therefore\) the radius of the water drop is \(6 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}\), that is \(6\ \text{mm}\).

stem: The susceptibility of magnetic material is \(\chi\) at 27°C. At what temperature its susceptibility will be \(\chi/3\) ?
solution:
For a paramagnetic material the susceptibility obeys Curie's law, being inversely proportional to the absolute temperature:

\(\chi = \dfrac{C}{T}\), so \(\chi T = \text{constant}\)

Hence for two temperatures

\(\chi_1 T_1 = \chi_2 T_2\)

Here \(\chi_1 = \chi\) at \(T_1 = 27^{\circ}\text{C} = 300\ \text{K}\), and \(\chi_2 = \dfrac{\chi}{3}\).

\(\chi \times 300 = \dfrac{\chi}{3} \times T_2\)

\(T_2 = 3 \times 300 = 900\ \text{K}\)

\(\therefore T_2 = 900\ \text{K}\), that is \(627^{\circ}\text{C}\). The susceptibility falls to a third of its value when the absolute temperature is trebled.

subtopic: Phasors and Types of AC Circuits
stem:
An alternating voltage source given by \(e = 140 \sin(314.2\,t)\) is connected across a pure resistor of \(50\ \Omega\). Determine :
(i) Frequency of the source.
(ii) RMS value of emf.
solution:
The source is \(e = 140\sin(314.2\,t)\), which compared with \(e = e_0\sin\omega t\) gives a peak emf \(e_0 = 140\ \text{V}\) and \(\omega = 314.2\ \text{rad/s}\).

**(i) Frequency of the source**

\(\omega = 2\pi n\), so \(n = \dfrac{\omega}{2\pi} = \dfrac{314.2}{2 \times 3.142}\)

\(n = 50\ \text{Hz}\)

**(ii) RMS value of emf**

\(e_{rms} = \dfrac{e_0}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{140}{1.414}\)

\(e_{rms} = 99\ \text{V}\)

\(\therefore\) the frequency is \(50\ \text{Hz}\) and the rms emf is about \(99\ \text{V}\). The value of the resistance is not needed for either part.

subtopic: Theorems of Parallel and Perpendicular Axes
stem: State and prove perpendicular axes theorem.
solution:
**Statement.** The moment of inertia of a plane lamina about an axis perpendicular to its plane is equal to the sum of its moments of inertia about two mutually perpendicular axes lying in the plane of the lamina, all three axes meeting at one point.

\(I_z = I_x + I_y\)

**Proof.** Let a lamina lie in the \(xy\) plane, with the \(z\) axis perpendicular to it through the origin O. Consider a mass element \(dm\) at the point \((x, y)\), at a distance \(r\) from O, so that

\(r^{2} = x^{2} + y^{2}\)

Its moment of inertia about the \(z\) axis is \(r^{2}\,dm\), and for the whole lamina

\(I_z = \displaystyle\int r^{2}\,dm = \int (x^{2} + y^{2})\,dm\)

\(I_z = \displaystyle\int y^{2}\,dm + \int x^{2}\,dm\)

Now \(y\) is the perpendicular distance of \(dm\) from the \(x\) axis and \(x\) is its perpendicular distance from the \(y\) axis, so these two integrals are \(I_x\) and \(I_y\).

\(\therefore I_z = I_x + I_y\)

The proof used \(z = 0\) for every element, so the theorem holds only for a plane lamina.

stem: On the basis of molecular theory, explain the phenomenon of surface tension.
solution:
On the molecular theory, surface tension arises from the cohesive forces between the molecules of a liquid.

Every molecule attracts every other molecule within a small distance called the range of molecular attraction, and the sphere of that radius drawn about a molecule is its sphere of influence.

**A molecule deep inside the liquid** has its sphere of influence entirely filled with liquid. It is pulled equally in all directions by its neighbours, so the resultant cohesive force on it is zero.

**A molecule at or near the surface** has part of its sphere of influence above the liquid, occupied by vapour, which is far less dense. It therefore has fewer molecules pulling it upward than downward, and experiences a **net inward force** perpendicular to the surface.

Because of this inward pull, work must be done against it to bring a molecule from the interior to the surface. A surface molecule therefore has greater potential energy than one inside, and the surface layer stores potential energy in proportion to its area.

A system in equilibrium takes the state of least potential energy, so the liquid surface tends to contract to the smallest possible area, behaving like a stretched elastic membrane. This tendency is surface tension, and it is why a free liquid drop takes a spherical shape.

stem: Show that all harmonics are present in the case of an air column vibrating in a pipe open at both the ends.
solution:
Consider an air column of length \(L\) in a pipe open at both ends. Both ends are free, so an **antinode** is formed at each end, and there is at least one node between them.

**Fundamental mode.** With one node at the middle, the length holds half a wavelength:

\(L = \dfrac{\lambda_1}{2}\), so \(\lambda_1 = 2L\)

\(n_1 = \dfrac{v}{\lambda_1} = \dfrac{v}{2L}\)

**First overtone.** With two nodes, the length holds one full wavelength:

\(L = \lambda_2\), so \(n_2 = \dfrac{v}{L} = 2\left(\dfrac{v}{2L}\right) = 2n_1\)

**Second overtone.** With three nodes, \(L = \dfrac{3\lambda_3}{2}\), so

\(n_3 = \dfrac{3v}{2L} = 3n_1\)

In general, with \(p\) nodes the length holds \(\dfrac{p\lambda}{2}\), giving

\(n_p = \dfrac{pv}{2L} = p\,n_1\), where \(p = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\)

\(\therefore\) the frequencies are in the ratio \(n_1 : n_2 : n_3 : \ldots = 1 : 2 : 3 : \ldots\), so **all** the harmonics, both even and odd, are present in a pipe open at both ends.

subtopic: Interference and Young's Double Slit Experiment
stem: What is interference of light? State any four conditions for obtaining well defined and steady interference pattern.
solution:
**Interference of light** is the phenomenon in which two light waves of the same frequency, travelling in nearly the same direction, superpose and redistribute the light energy, producing a steady pattern of alternately bright and dark regions called interference fringes. No energy is created or destroyed; it is only redistributed, the energy missing from the dark fringes appearing in the bright ones.

Four conditions for a well defined and steady interference pattern:

**1.** The two sources must be **coherent**, that is, they must emit waves of the same frequency with a constant phase difference between them. In practice this means deriving both from a single source.

**2.** The two sources must be **narrow** and very close together, otherwise the fringes overlap and the pattern is washed out.

**3.** The amplitudes of the two interfering waves should be **equal or nearly equal**, so that the dark fringes are as nearly dark as possible and the contrast is good.

**4.** The light should be **monochromatic**, otherwise each wavelength forms its own set of fringes of different width and the patterns overlap into coloured bands.

subtopic: p-n Junction Diode as a Rectifier
stem: With the help of a neat circuit diagram, explain the working of a half wave rectifier. Draw input and output waveforms.
solution:
**Circuit.** The secondary of a transformer is connected in series with a p-n junction diode and a load resistance \(R_L\). The a.c. voltage to be rectified appears across the series combination, and the rectified output is taken across \(R_L\).

**Working.** The diode conducts only when it is forward biased.

During the **positive half cycle** of the input, the p side of the diode is at the higher potential, so the diode is forward biased. Its resistance is very small, current flows through the load, and an output voltage appears across \(R_L\) following the shape of the input.

During the **negative half cycle**, the polarity reverses and the diode is reverse biased. Its resistance is very high, practically no current flows, and the output voltage across \(R_L\) is almost zero.

The diode therefore passes only one half of each cycle, and the load current is unidirectional though pulsating. Because only half of each cycle is used, the arrangement is called a half wave rectifier.

**Waveforms.** The input waveform is a full sine wave, alternately positive and negative. The output waveform consists only of the positive humps of that sine wave, with a flat zero in place of each negative half cycle.

stem: Obtain an expression for orbital magnetic moment of an electron revolving around the nucleus of an atom.
solution:
Consider an electron of charge \(e\) and mass \(m_e\) moving in a circular orbit of radius \(r\) with speed \(v\) around the nucleus.

The revolving electron is equivalent to a current loop. The time for one revolution is

\(T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v}\)

so the equivalent current, being the charge passing a point per unit time, is

\(I = \dfrac{e}{T} = \dfrac{ev}{2\pi r}\)

The magnetic moment of a current loop is the product of the current and the area it encloses:

\(M_{orb} = I A = \dfrac{ev}{2\pi r} \times \pi r^{2}\)

\(\therefore M_{orb} = \dfrac{evr}{2}\)

This can be written in terms of the orbital angular momentum \(L = m_e v r\). Multiplying and dividing by \(m_e\),

\(M_{orb} = \dfrac{e}{2m_e}(m_e v r) = \dfrac{e}{2m_e}L\)

The ratio \(\dfrac{M_{orb}}{L} = \dfrac{e}{2m_e}\) is called the gyromagnetic ratio. The magnetic moment is directed opposite to the angular momentum, because the electron's charge is negative.

subtopic: Phasors and Types of AC Circuits
stem:
Define the terms :
(a) Inductive reactance
(b) Capacitive reactance
(c) Impedance
solution:
**(a) Inductive reactance.** The opposition offered by a pure inductor to the flow of alternating current through it. It arises from the back emf induced in the coil by the changing current, and is measured in ohm.

\(X_L = \omega L = 2\pi n L\)

It is directly proportional to the frequency, so an inductor blocks high frequencies and passes direct current freely.

**(b) Capacitive reactance.** The opposition offered by a pure capacitor to the flow of alternating current in the circuit, measured in ohm.

\(X_C = \dfrac{1}{\omega C} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi n C}\)

It is inversely proportional to the frequency, so a capacitor passes high frequencies and blocks direct current altogether.

**(c) Impedance.** The effective opposition offered by a circuit containing resistance and reactance together to the flow of alternating current, measured in ohm. For a series LCR circuit

\(Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + (X_L - X_C)^{2}}\)

and the rms current is \(I_{rms} = \dfrac{e_{rms}}{Z}\).

stem: A parallel plate capacitor filled with air has an area \(6\ \text{cm}^{2}\) and the plate separation is 2 mm. Calculate its capacity.
solution:
For a parallel plate capacitor with air between the plates,

\(C = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}\)

Here \(A = 6\ \text{cm}^{2} = 6 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^{2}\), \(d = 2\ \text{mm} = 2 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}\) and \(\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{C}^{2}/\text{Nm}^{2}\).

\(C = \dfrac{8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 6 \times 10^{-4}}{2 \times 10^{-3}}\)

\(C = \dfrac{53.1 \times 10^{-16}}{2 \times 10^{-3}}\)

\(C = 2.655 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{F}\)

\(\therefore\) the capacity of the capacitor is \(2.655 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{F}\), that is \(2.655\ \text{pF}\).

stem: Two resistances \(X\) and \(Y\) in the two gaps of a meterbridge give a null point dividing the wire in the ratio 4 : 6. If both resistances are increased by \(30\ \Omega\), the null point divides the wire in the ratio 5 : 6. Calculate the value of \(X\) and \(Y\).
solution:
In a metre bridge at balance, the two resistances are in the ratio of the two lengths of the wire:

\(\dfrac{X}{Y} = \dfrac{l_1}{l_2}\)

**First balance.** The null point divides the wire in the ratio \(4 : 6\), so

\(\dfrac{X}{Y} = \dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}\), giving \(X = \dfrac{2Y}{3}\)   ... (1)

**Second balance.** Each resistance is increased by \(30\ \Omega\) and the ratio becomes \(5 : 6\):

\(\dfrac{X + 30}{Y + 30} = \dfrac{5}{6}\)

\(6(X + 30) = 5(Y + 30)\)

\(6X + 180 = 5Y + 150\)   ... (2)

Substituting (1) into (2),

\(6\left(\dfrac{2Y}{3}\right) + 180 = 5Y + 150\)

\(4Y + 180 = 5Y + 150\)

\(Y = 30\)

From (1), \(X = \dfrac{2 \times 30}{3} = 20\)

\(\therefore X = 20\ \Omega\) and \(Y = 30\ \Omega\).

Check: \(20 : 30 = 4 : 6\), and \(50 : 60 = 5 : 6\), so both balances are satisfied.

stem: Calculate the shortest wavelength of Paschen series and the longest wavelength of Balmer series for hydrogen atom.
solution:
For hydrogen the wave number of a spectral line is

\(\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{n^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{m^{2}}\right)\)

with \(R = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\).

**Shortest wavelength of the Paschen series.** The Paschen series has \(n = 3\), and the shortest wavelength is the series limit, \(m = \infty\):

\(\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{9} - 0\right) = \dfrac{R}{9}\)

\(\lambda = \dfrac{9}{R} = \dfrac{9}{1.097 \times 10^{7}} = 8.204 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}\)

**Longest wavelength of the Balmer series.** The Balmer series has \(n = 2\), and the longest wavelength comes from the smallest energy jump, \(m = 3\):

\(\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{9}\right) = R\left(\dfrac{5}{36}\right)\)

\(\lambda = \dfrac{36}{5R} = \dfrac{36}{5 \times 1.097 \times 10^{7}} = 6.563 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}\)

\(\therefore\) the shortest Paschen wavelength is \(8204\ \text{Å}\) and the longest Balmer wavelength is \(6563\ \text{Å}\).

chapter: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
stem: Calculate the current flowing through two long parallel wires carrying equal currents and separated by a distance of 1.35 cm experiencing a force per unit length of \(4.76 \times 10^{-2}\) N/m.
solution:
Two long parallel wires carrying currents \(I_1\) and \(I_2\) a distance \(d\) apart exert on each other a force per unit length

\(\dfrac{F}{L} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}\)

The currents are equal, so \(I_1 = I_2 = I\) and

\(\dfrac{F}{L} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I^{2}}{2\pi d}\)

Rearranging,

\(I^{2} = \dfrac{2\pi d}{\mu_0}\left(\dfrac{F}{L}\right)\)

Here \(d = 1.35\ \text{cm} = 1.35 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{m}\), \(\dfrac{F}{L} = 4.76 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{N/m}\) and \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\ \text{Wb/Am}\).

\(I^{2} = \dfrac{2\pi \times 1.35 \times 10^{-2}}{4\pi \times 10^{-7}} \times 4.76 \times 10^{-2}\)

\(I^{2} = \dfrac{1.35 \times 10^{-2}}{2 \times 10^{-7}} \times 4.76 \times 10^{-2}\)

\(I^{2} = 67500 \times 4.76 \times 10^{-2} = 3213\)

\(I = \sqrt{3213} = 56.68\ \text{A}\)

\(\therefore\) the current in each wire is about \(56.7\ \text{A}\).

stem: An emf of 90 mV is induced in the winding of a coil, when current in a nearby coil is increasing at the rate of 4.5 A/s. What is the mutual inductance of the two coils?
solution:
When the current in one coil changes, the emf induced in a neighbouring coil is

\(e = M\dfrac{dI}{dt}\)

where \(M\) is the mutual inductance of the pair. Rearranging,

\(M = \dfrac{e}{dI/dt}\)

Here \(e = 90\ \text{mV} = 90 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{V}\) and \(\dfrac{dI}{dt} = 4.5\ \text{A/s}\).

\(M = \dfrac{90 \times 10^{-3}}{4.5}\)

\(M = 0.02\ \text{H}\)

\(\therefore\) the mutual inductance of the two coils is \(0.02\ \text{H}\), that is \(20\ \text{mH}\).

chapter: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Mean Free Path and Pressure of an Ideal Gas
stem: Derive an expression for pressure exerted by a gas on the basis of kinetic theory of gases.
solution:
Consider \(N\) molecules of an ideal gas, each of mass \(m\), enclosed in a cubical vessel of side \(L\). Take one molecule moving with velocity components \(v_x, v_y, v_z\).

**Momentum given to one wall.** The molecule strikes the wall perpendicular to the \(x\) axis and rebounds elastically, so its \(x\) momentum changes from \(mv_x\) to \(-mv_x\). The momentum transferred to the wall in one impact is

\(\Delta p = 2mv_x\)

Between two successive impacts on the same wall the molecule travels a distance \(2L\) along \(x\), so the time between impacts is

\(\Delta t = \dfrac{2L}{v_x}\)

**Force due to one molecule.**

\(f = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{2mv_x}{2L/v_x} = \dfrac{mv_x^{2}}{L}\)

**Total force and pressure.** Summing over all \(N\) molecules and dividing by the area \(L^{2}\),

\(p = \dfrac{1}{L^{3}}\sum m v_x^{2} = \dfrac{m}{V}\sum v_x^{2}\)

since \(L^{3} = V\). Writing the mean square \(x\) velocity as \(\overline{v_x^{2}}\),

\(p = \dfrac{mN\overline{v_x^{2}}}{V}\)

The motion is random, so no direction is favoured and

\(\overline{v_x^{2}} = \overline{v_y^{2}} = \overline{v_z^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{3}\overline{v^{2}}\)

Substituting,

\(\therefore p = \dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{mN\overline{v^{2}}}{V} = \dfrac{1}{3}\rho\,\overline{v^{2}}\)

where \(\rho = \dfrac{mN}{V}\) is the density of the gas. The pressure of a gas is one third of the product of its density and the mean square speed of its molecules.

subtopic: Acceleration, Velocity and Displacement in S.H.M.
stem: State differential equation of linear S.H.M. hence obtain an expression for acceleration, velocity and displacement of a particle performing S.H.M.
solution:
**Differential equation of linear S.H.M.** In linear S.H.M. the restoring force is proportional to the displacement from the mean position and is directed toward it:

\(F = -kx\)

Writing \(F = ma\) and \(a = \dfrac{d^{2}x}{dt^{2}}\),

\(m\dfrac{d^{2}x}{dt^{2}} + kx = 0\), or \(\dfrac{d^{2}x}{dt^{2}} + \omega^{2}x = 0\) with \(\omega^{2} = \dfrac{k}{m}\)

**Acceleration.** From the equation itself,

\(a = \dfrac{d^{2}x}{dt^{2}} = -\omega^{2}x\)

The acceleration is proportional to the displacement and oppositely directed; it is zero at the mean position and greatest at the extreme positions.

**Velocity.** Write \(a = v\dfrac{dv}{dx}\), so that

\(v\,dv = -\omega^{2}x\,dx\)

Integrating, \(\dfrac{v^{2}}{2} = -\dfrac{\omega^{2}x^{2}}{2} + C\). At the extreme position \(x = A\) the particle is momentarily at rest, \(v = 0\), which gives \(C = \dfrac{\omega^{2}A^{2}}{2}\). Hence

\(v^{2} = \omega^{2}(A^{2} - x^{2})\)

\(\therefore v = \pm\,\omega\sqrt{A^{2} - x^{2}}\)

The speed is greatest, \(A\omega\), at the mean position, and zero at the extremes.

**Displacement.** Write \(v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = \omega\sqrt{A^{2} - x^{2}}\), so

\(\dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{A^{2} - x^{2}}} = \omega\,dt\)

Integrating, \(\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x}{A}\right) = \omega t + \phi\), where \(\phi\) is the constant of integration, called the initial phase.

\(\therefore x = A\sin(\omega t + \phi)\)

stem:
With the help of neat diagram explain construction of a transformer.
Calculate energy required to build up current of 1A in an inductor of inductance 20 mH.
solution:
**Construction of a transformer.** A transformer consists of two coils of insulated copper wire, the **primary** and the **secondary**, wound on a common **soft iron core**. The core is built of thin sheets, called laminations, insulated from one another by a coat of varnish, and the whole is assembled as a closed magnetic circuit.

The input a.c. supply is given to the primary and the output is taken from the secondary. The two coils are electrically insulated from each other; energy passes from one to the other only through the changing magnetic flux in the core, which is the phenomenon of mutual induction.

The soft iron core is used because its high permeability confines almost the whole of the flux produced by the primary and carries it through the secondary, and because its low retentivity and low coercivity mean little energy is wasted in taking it round its hysteresis loop fifty times a second. The core is laminated to break up the paths available to eddy currents, which would otherwise heat the core and waste energy.

If \(N_p\) and \(N_s\) are the numbers of turns, the emfs are in the ratio \(\dfrac{e_s}{e_p} = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p}\).

**Energy stored in the inductor.** The energy stored in an inductor carrying a current \(I\) is

\(W = \dfrac{1}{2}LI^{2}\)

Here \(L = 20\ \text{mH} = 20 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{H}\) and \(I = 1\ \text{A}\).

\(W = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 20 \times 10^{-3} \times (1)^{2}\)

\(W = 10^{-2}\ \text{J}\)

\(\therefore\) the energy required is \(0.01\ \text{J}\), that is \(10\ \text{mJ}\).

chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem:
Draw a neat schematic diagram of a photo cell.
The photoelectric work function for a metal is 4.2 eV. Find threshold wavelength.
solution:
**Schematic diagram of a photo cell.** A photo cell consists of an evacuated glass or quartz bulb containing two electrodes. The **cathode** is a semi-cylindrical metal plate coated on its inner surface with a photosensitive metal of low work function, such as caesium. The **anode** is a thin straight wire or rod placed along the axis of the cathode, positioned so as not to block the light. The two electrodes are connected through an external circuit containing a battery, which keeps the anode positive, and a microammeter to read the photocurrent. Light enters through a quartz window and falls on the cathode.

When light of frequency above the threshold falls on the cathode, photoelectrons are emitted; the positive anode collects them and the microammeter registers a current proportional to the intensity of the light.

**Threshold wavelength.** At the threshold, the photon energy just equals the work function:

\(\phi_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0}\), so \(\lambda_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\phi_0}\)

Here \(\phi_0 = 4.2\ \text{eV} = 4.2 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J} = 6.72 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}\).

\(\lambda_0 = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^{8}}{6.72 \times 10^{-19}}\)

\(\lambda_0 = \dfrac{1.989 \times 10^{-25}}{6.72 \times 10^{-19}}\)

\(\lambda_0 = 2.96 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}\)

\(\therefore\) the threshold wavelength is \(2.96 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}\), that is about \(2960\ \text{Å}\), which lies in the ultraviolet.

chapter: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
stem: Obtain an expression for magnetic induction of a toroid of N no. of turns about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to plane.
solution:
A **toroid** is a solenoid bent into the form of a closed ring, so that its magnetic field is confined entirely within the core and there are no ends from which flux can leak.

Let the toroid have \(N\) closely wound turns carrying a current \(I\), and let \(r\) be the mean radius of the ring.

By symmetry the field inside the core has the same magnitude at every point of a circle of radius \(r\) drawn concentric with the toroid, and is everywhere tangential to that circle. Take this circle as the Amperian loop.

Applying Ampere's circuital law,

\(\oint \vec{B} \cdot \overrightarrow{dl} = \mu_0 I_{enclosed}\)

Since \(\vec{B}\) is parallel to \(\overrightarrow{dl}\) everywhere on the loop and constant in magnitude,

\(B \oint dl = B(2\pi r)\)

The loop encloses all \(N\) turns, each carrying current \(I\), so \(I_{enclosed} = NI\).

\(B(2\pi r) = \mu_0 NI\)

\(\therefore B = \dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{2\pi r}\)

Writing \(n = \dfrac{N}{2\pi r}\) for the number of turns per unit length, this becomes \(B = \mu_0 n I\), the same as for a long solenoid. Outside the toroid, both for a loop drawn inside the inner radius and for one drawn beyond the outer radius, the enclosed current is zero, so the field there is zero.

stem: A Carnot refrigerator operates between 150 K and 200 K, calculate its coefficient of performance.
solution:
The coefficient of performance of a Carnot refrigerator working between a cold reservoir at \(T_C\) and a hot reservoir at \(T_H\) is

\(\text{K} = \dfrac{T_C}{T_H - T_C}\)

Here \(T_C = 150\ \text{K}\) and \(T_H = 200\ \text{K}\).

\(\text{K} = \dfrac{150}{200 - 150} = \dfrac{150}{50}\)

\(\text{K} = 3\)

\(\therefore\) the coefficient of performance is \(3\). The refrigerator removes three joules of heat from the cold reservoir for every joule of work supplied to it.
